newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss to reveal more accounts in Jewish asset hunt.
newsitem.headline: Swiss to reveal more accounts in Jewish asset hunt.

text.p: The head of the Swiss Bankers Association said on Friday that details of some 20,000 bank accounts opened by Swiss citizens before 1945 would be published to help the hunt for the wealth of Jews murdered by Hitler.
Georg Krayer said account holders' names would be revealed, including on the Internet, as part of the "cleaning process" over Swiss wartime links with Nazi Germany.
"We should publish everything and everything," he told reporters after a banking news conference.
But he said the accounts, mostly passbook savings, were unlikely to yield much in the search for Holocaust victims' assets, which Jewish groups allege Swiss banks plundered..

"It could be a figure of roughly 20,000. But this is add on (to non-Swiss accounts already found)," he told reporters. "They are domestic accounts. It seems most of these are those godparent accounts in passbook savings form."
He said most held only small sums of money.
These accounts were not covered by the last sweep of Swiss banks which Krayer said had found about $30 million in unclaimed funds in some 1,000 accounts opened in the names of non-Swiss.
Passbooks were a common form of savings during the wartime era, but do not technically count as bank accounts under terms of the search for dormant Jewish wealth.

The news comes ahead of an audit at a first group of five banks by an independent commission headed by former U.S. Federal Reserve chief Paul Volcker and empowered to waive Swiss banking secrecy rules in order to scrutinise wartime accounts.

Jewish groups maintain super-secretive Swiss banks have kept thousands of heirs and survivors from collecting money deposited in Switzerland by Jews seeking to avoid Nazi confiscation of their wealth before or during the Holocaust.
Landlocked Switzerland's neutrality in the midst of warring Europe has come under Western cas little more than collaboration with Nazis under a different name.
Krayer said no new accounts opened by possible Holocaust victims had turned up.
Volcker, at a Geneva news conference last week, urged Swiss banks to publish the names of wartime account holders as soon as possible. Krayer said this would be done "by the end of summer".
Only a few months ago, top Swiss bankers were saying that it would be nearly impossible to trace all the money of murdered Jews because the bulk had been deposited under other names.
Before the audit, which is expected to start shortly, there was no word on the presence of another 20,000 wartime accounts which may include Jewish assets deposited in trustee names.
Information and documents about wartime accounts have been surfacing in Switzerland only lately.
Recently, cantonal records in Lausanne revealed thousands of individual bank accounts, held mostly by Swiss but also by some foreigners, closed by banks without the knowledge of owners.
It remains unclear what happened to money in wartime accounts that were closed, but much apparently went to charity.
Volcker has said that tracing accounts that were supposed to be dormant but have been removed in the past 50 years will be one of the main challenges facing the auditors.
Switzerland has yet to come up with a legal and more flexible mechanism allowing fast payments on claims.
"We have very good people from the legal side working on that and we hope we can find a solution as soon as possible," Krayer said.
"Some ideas suggest having an international agreement but that would take more time than everybody would like. Some people say we could do it in a private arbitration form," he added.

"But if you have one Felix Mueller and ten people show up, what do you do? If you have one person saying 'I'm the son of Felix Mueller, another saying 'I'm the grandson', another saying 'I'm the only survivor of the Mueller family', what do you do?"
